To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the statistical regime of the EU, and the European statistical system, have been constructed in order to create commensurability and comparability of the member states.
The European Statistical System (ESS) is a highly complex system that is based on a network of national and international institutions and organizations.

(1) the statistical regime is a crucial part of European integration; (2) the statistical regime has become commensurable and commensurable; (3) the statistical regime makes member states commensurable and thus comparable; (4) the statistical regime reduces complexity; (5) the statistical regime produces a Europe-wide space; and (6) the statistical regime can be understood as a European governmentality.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the making of Europe as a statistical object.
the following questions: How is Europe made comparable and commensurate?
the question how the European Union (EU) and its member states are being governed.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

numbers are crucial for modern systems of government because they make objects commensurate and therefore comparable and reduce complexity, which in turn allows for a more efficient use of resources and a better control of the population.
the European statistical apparatus is an important and powerful tool for making the member states comparable and commensurate.
the European Union has become commensurate and, to some extent, comparable.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we are not in a post-statistical world.

numbers have been crucial for the making of a Europe that has become commensurate and thus comparable, but also for the making of the European Union as a political project that can be made visible, and thus governable, in the form of numbers.

we have shown that the making of a statistical regime in Europe has been part of a process of European integration and that the statistical regime has been an important instrument in the making of the EU.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the statistical apparatus is not only a technical instrument but also a social and political one.
the statistical regime is an important part of the European project and that it is a regime in its own right.

the European statistical system has been built up through an ongoing process of standardisation, which in turn is dependent upon a process of homogenisation of the statistical practices of national statistical offices.
